SHENZHEN: An international free trade forum in an age of tariffs - and the prospect of an unprecedented meeting between three of the world’s most powerful leaders.
articles.body:
China hosts APEC for the first time in 12 years. High-profile sideline diplomacy is drawing attention amid questions over whether the forum in Shenzhen can deliver more than symbolism.

SHENZHEN: An international free trade forum in an age of tariffs - and the prospect of an unprecedented meeting between three of the world’s most powerful leaders.

Leaders of the 21 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies gather in Shenzhen this week, with eyes peeled for the first three-way talks between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday (Nov 19).

Trump is also due to meet Xi separately, the White House has said, in what will be their third meeting this year as the world’s two largest economies continue to grapple with trade and technology disputes.

For host China, the summit is an opportunity to champion its vision of an open, integrated Asia-Pacific.

But amid the flurry of high-stakes diplomacy on the sidelines, questions remain over what APEC itself can deliver - and whether a forum built to promote free trade can retain its relevance in an increasingly fractured global economy.

ONE SUMMIT, COMPETING PRIORITIES

APEC was set up in 1989 to promote trade and investment across the Pacific.

Member economies include the US, China and Russia, alongside Japan, South Korea, Australia and several Southeast Asian states such as Singapore and Indonesia.

Taken together, they account for about 60 per cent of global gross domestic product and nearly half of world trade, according to the APEC Secretariat.

Decisions are made by consensus and commitments are voluntary.

China is hosting for the first time in 12 years, with the Economic Leaders’ Meeting taking place on Wednesday (Nov 18) and Thursday.

Beijing wants the summit to affirm its commitment to open trade, analysts said.

It has set “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together” as this year’s theme, with openness, innovation and cooperation as priorities.

Chinese officials have said they want leaders to adopt a Shenzhen declaration, along with a document on the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) and a roadmap on artificial intelligence and the digital economy.

The FTAAP, a proposed free trade zone spanning all 21 APEC economies, was first endorsed by the bloc’s leaders in 2006 but has yet to materialise.

“This year marks the 20th anniversary (of the FTAAP). I think the Chinese side will push for a roadmap,” Xu Qinduo, a senior fellow at Pangoal Institution, a Beijing-based think-tank, told CNA.

“China wants to reaffirm that it is committed to an open Asia-Pacific region,” he added.

Chinese commerce ministry officials said at a briefing on Monday that nearly 50 economic and trade outcomes - such as roadmaps and pilot projects - had already been achieved during China's year as APEC host, with about half focused on digital trade and AI.

Asked by CNA where members had found consensus, Chen Chao, director-general of the ministry's Department of International Trade and Economic Affairs, pointed to a framework on trade digitalisation that China is developing with other members.

"The aim is to agree on guidelines for digital trade cooperation that suit the realities of the Asia-Pacific and can actually be put into practice," he said, describing the framework as a major deliverable for the leaders' meeting.

But any declaration needs agreement from all members, and that might be a formidable task amid growing trade tensions and diverging approaches to economic integration.

The top US official for APEC said in May that the FTAAP is “more an agenda than it is a kind of destination”.

Last year’s leaders’ declaration, adopted in South Korea, dropped longstanding references to the World Trade Organization and the multilateral trading system.

China wants to use the summit to burnish its image on the global stage, analysts said.

“(Beijing) wants to project an image of a responsible, stable great power,” Lim Tai Wei, an East Asian affairs observer and professor at Japan’s Soka University, told CNA.

“This will be an opportunity, a coming-out party for China.”

Washington’s priorities lie elsewhere.

Chief among them is ensuring China follows through on its existing trade commitments, particularly purchases of American agricultural goods, said Dexter Tiff Roberts, a non-resident senior fellow at the Global China Hub of US think-tank Atlantic Council.

After Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the White House said China had committed to buying at least US$17 billion of American farm goods a year, on top of soybeans. In September, the two sides agreed to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of each other’s goods, without setting a timeline.

China bought US$7.2 billion of non-soybean US farm goods between January and September, according to a Reuters analysis, raising doubts about whether it can meet its purchasing commitment.

China’s commerce ministry said on Nov 5 that it was open to buying more US farm goods, but only if tariff cuts are implemented.

SIDESHOWS IN SHENZHEN

But the formal APEC agenda is not necessarily what draws leaders to the summit.

“The heads of state for each country, when they meet, will pick up their entire agenda, not focus on the APEC agenda,” said Drew Thompson, a senior fellow at the Singapore-based think-tank S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS).

“Their own side meetings with other leaders are as important to them as the attention-grabbing great-power dialogues,” he told CNA.

Two potential meetings on the summit’s margins in Shenzhen have drawn particular attention.

One is between Trump and Xi.

US officials have said the two leaders will hold a bilateral meeting and working lunch on Thursday.

The truce was extended on Nov 9 and now runs until Jan 10 next year.

“I think best case, the truce renewal continues beyond Jan 10,” said Thompson.

But the prospect of a more comprehensive agreement remains uncertain, with Washington pressing Beijing to honour its purchasing commitments and China seeking further tariff relief.

AI is another area where the two powers differ in their approach.

Beijing is seeking a greater role in shaping global AI governance, while Washington has resisted efforts to regulate AI through international bodies.

The other highly anticipated event is the three-way meeting involving Trump, Xi and Putin.

Following earlier confirmation from the White House and the Kremlin, China’s foreign ministry said on Monday that Xi will hold a “China-Russia-US heads of state meeting” with Putin and Trump in Shenzhen on Nov 19.

It will be the very first trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three nuclear powers.

But the exact agenda remains uncertain, as the three men will enter the talks with differing priorities shaped by their respective national interests.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Monday that the three leaders will exchange views on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major country relations.

Trump, meanwhile, has been more explicit about his priorities.

“We're talking a lot of things, including denuclearisation, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," Trump said on Nov 8.

US officials have since said Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals and will raise the war in Iran, but is not expected to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine.

“The president believes this (nuclear arms) proliferation is very dangerous,” said White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales on Nov 13.

Russia has signalled that Ukraine is its priority. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Nov 12 that Putin and Trump would continue discussing a settlement when they meet in Shenzhen, Russian state media reported.

US officials have said no separate meeting between Trump and Putin is scheduled.

China has signalled that it does not want Ukraine on the discussion table. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who met Xi in Beijing on Oct 30, told German broadcaster ARD that the Chinese leader expected to meet Trump and Putin in Shenzhen, but not to discuss the war.

Xi described it as a European conflict that needs Europeans at the negotiating table, Steinmeier said.

The Wall Street Journal has also reported that Xi is unwilling to join a meeting that allows open discussion of issues such as nuclear arms control, and wants the outcomes settled in advance.

China’s foreign ministry said last month that it would not be reasonable or realistic to ask China to join trilateral nuclear disarmament talks at this stage.

“Putin … he wants this to happen. China is probably the most hesitant,” said Atlantic Council’s Roberts, who spoke to CNA before the meeting was confirmed. He expects the meeting to be a “showcase” with “no real teeth”.

From Beijing’s perspective, the world’s affairs should not be settled by a few big powers, said Pangoal Institution’s Xu.

“I don’t think Singapore, (for instance), welcomes a G2 world or a G3 world,” said Xu, who is also an adjunct professor at Renmin University of China.

G2, or Group of Two, and G3 refer to the idea of two or three major powers jointly steering global affairs, respectively.

“After all, the APEC summit is about the economy, is about trade. It’s not about international security,” he said.

Even so, the mere fact that such a meeting takes place would be a “very powerful symbol”, said Soka University’s Lim.

Meetings between the great powers “will probably set the tone for international and global trade”, he added.

SPEED DATING OR SUBSTANCE?

Analysts were divided on what the APEC forum itself can achieve.

“APEC is not really fit for purpose, and I think it’s struggling to maintain its relevance in an era where economic integration is seen as a national security threat or vulnerability,” said Thompson.

“This is speed dating for heads of state, and that’s its value.”

Lim said disruptions to supplies of critical minerals, rare earths and energy have “put a lot of countries on edge”.

But ultimately, most economies in the region, from Southeast Asia to Latin America, want the same thing from the summit, said Pangoal Institution’s Xu.

“We are all for more trade, more investment, and more globalisation, more regional integration, rather than more tariffs,” he said, noting that Singapore is “playing a prominent role” in promoting digital trade.

To him, a successful summit would reinforce the message of regional openness.

“The goal is more trade. The goal is more engagement, rather than isolation, rather than rivalry,” he said.

“That would be good enough, probably.”

articles.title: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthis are gaining ground and their advance could have dangerous consequences, writes the BBC's security correspondent.
articles.preview: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden. Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world. Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.
articles.body:
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.

Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.

Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.

The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.

Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.

But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.

When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.

The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.

But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.

On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.

Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."

He warns that if the port of Aden â a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants â was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".

But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.

"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."

"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."

It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.

The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.

He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.

"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.

"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

articles.title: Gilbert Houngbo re-elected to lead UN labour agency for second term
articles.summary: Former Togo prime minister Gilbert Houngbo has secured a second five-year term as head of the UN's International Labour Organization. His re-election came after his only challenger, Spain's Labour Minister, withdrew at the last minute. Houngbo says he's ready to continue the agency's work.
articles.preview: Former Togo prime minister Gilbert Houngbo has secured a second five-year term as head of the UN's International Labour Organization. His re-election came after his only challenger, Spain's Labour Minister, withdrew at the last minute. Houngbo says he's ready to continue the agency's work.
articles.body:
International Labour Organization

Former Togolese prime minister Gilbert Houngbo was re-elected Monday as head of the United Nations' labour agency after the only rival candidate pulled out at the last minute. Houngbo was re-elected for a second, five-year term as director-general of the International Labour Organization, starting on October 1 next year, after Spanish Labour Minister Yolanda Diaz Perez withdrew.

Houngbo received 51 votes out of 56 at the meeting of the ILO's governing body, at the UN agency's Geneva headquarters. There were five abstentions, an ILO spokeswoman told AFP. "More than a century after its founding, our organisation remains charged with a mission that is more relevant than ever: to promote social justice as the foundation for universal and lasting peace," said Houngbo, 65.

"Faced with the uncertainties of the world, we have a duty to defend human dignity, promote social justice and foster dialogue between nations, workers and employers." He said that among the challenges shaping the future, "none perhaps is more decisive than artificial intelligence", saying AI would open up new possibilities but also raise fundamental questions about jobs and skills.

He said the ILO must be at the forefront in "ensuring that technological progress remains at the service of humanity". Before the vote, Diaz Perez announced that she was pulling out, to avoid divisions within the trade union movement. In a statement on Bluesky, she lamented that the current ILO leadership had "plunged the organisation into the deepest financial crisis in its history". She said the general secretary of the International Trade Union Confederation and the spokesperson of the ILO Workers' Group had chosen to stick with Houngbo, "against the feeling of a large part of the world's trade union movement, which they have denied the freedom to vote". "I will not divide the trade union movement."

Former Peruvian foreign minister Javier Gonzalez-Olaechea, the only other declared candidate, pulled out of the race on November 4. The ILO has been going through a turbulent period for several months. A decline in international funding, particularly from the United States, has forced the organisation to undertake reforms including job cuts.

Founded in 1919, the ILO has 187 member states which, uniquely in the UN system, are represented by governments, employers and workers. The ILO aims to promote rights at work, encourage good employment opportunities, enhance social protection and strengthen dialogue on work-related issues.

articles.title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of attempted ‘coup’
articles.summary: Rivals call for investigation into reports that PM's office tried to frame Arab parties.
articles.preview: Political rivals call for investigation regarding media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to frame Arab party members ahead of the elections. Israeli opposition leaders have denounced an “attempted coup” by outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The accusations on Monday came in response to media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to falsely incriminate members of an Arab-led party before last month’s election, in which the premier’s Likud party was voted out of office.
articles.body:
Political rivals call for investigation regarding media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to frame Arab party members ahead of the elections.

Israeli opposition leaders have denounced an “attempted coup” by outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The accusations on Monday came in response to media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to falsely incriminate members of an Arab-led party before last month’s election, in which the premier’s Likud party was voted out of office.

“As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn’t an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup,” opposition leader Yair Lapid said on social media.

Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, called police with a complaint about members of the Ra’am party.

Norden reportedly pointed officers to a purported intelligence source – a former employee of Netanyahu’s office – who provided information that led to the arrest of three Ra’am members. They were later released after police determined the allegations were unfounded.

Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Sunday that the head of the Shin Bet domestic security service tried to wiretap leaders of the Arab-led Joint List, but the attorney general refused due to a lack of evidence.

Israeli police said in response that they will “review the decision-making and information-transmission process”. Likud has issued a statement denying the reports.

Following the vote, Netanyahu accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record 19 seats in the Knesset.

‘Dark regime’

Yousef Jabareen, the leader of Joint List also decried “an attempted coup by Netanyahu,” and labelled the allegations regarding Shin Bet as “conduct characteristic of dark regimes”.

Ra’am deputy and former police chief Yoav Segalovitz called for an urgent investigation.

“Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now,” he wrote on social media.

Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, wrote that departing prime minister was “a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy”.

Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s opposition grouping secured the 61 seats required to form a government. However, Joint List and Raam have indicated they support Eisenkot to lead a coalition.

articles.title: Incoming Texas governor to reverse terror designation for Muslim civil liberties group
articles.summary: Incoming Texas governor to reverse terror designation for Muslim civil liberties group Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 15:57 Gina Hinojosa said cracking down on nonprofits does not increase public safety Texas Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa appears with supporters outside the Austin Recreation Center before polls closed on Election Day, on 3 November 2026, in Austin, Texas (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images via AFP) Off The Democratic governor-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, has revealed she will reverse her predecessor's designation of the largest Muslim civil liberties group in the US as a terrorist organisation. In an interview published by The Washington Post on Saturday, Hinojosa, who handily beat three-term Governor Greg Abbott in the midterm elections earlier this month to become the first Hispanic woman in the role, said she would withdraw the executive order blacklisting the Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair). “We have to use public safety measures for public safety," she said. Hinojosa will be sworn into office in January. Civil rights groups in the state welcomed the move, the local station in Austin, Fox7, reported. "Greg Abbott used his office to fuel anti-Muslim hostility and intimidate the organizations defending their communities' rights," Sam Robles, executive director of the Texas Nonprofit Protection Network, said in a statement. "Abbott’s politically motivated designation of CAIR as a terrorist organization was another escalation in a campaign that sought to portray Muslim civic participation and advocacy as a public safety threat." Almost a year ago to the day, Abbott announced that he was designating the Muslim Brotherhood as well as Cair as foreign terrorist organisations and transnational criminal organisations. As a result, both groups were barred "from purchasing or acquiring land" in Texas. The proclamation gave the state's attorney general leeway to sue the groups accordingly. Aipac spent $55m on losing congressional candidates in midterm elections: Report as a Republican endorsed by President Donald Trump. He lost earlier this month to Democrat James Talarico, when the state's entire governing structure went from deep red Republican to Democratic blue, from the governor to the lieutenant governor, the attorney general, and the state legislature. The man primarily responsible for the promotion of anti-Muslim Brotherhood and anti-Cair narratives, Senator Ted Cruz, remains the sole Republican in power. Cruz has said the Muslim Brotherhood - whose popularity remains high in parts of the Arab world because of its combination of Islamic religious tradition, political activism and social welfare programming - was a threat to US national security. The movement does not have a defined control centre as it did for much of the 20th century in Egypt, where it began. One of its "offshoots" that Cruz repeatedly references is Hamas in Gaza, which is already designated as a terrorist organisation in the US. But Hamas does not act outside of the occupied Palestinian territories and Israel. 'Sharia law' Abbott's executive order specifically named Nihad Awad, the executive director of Cair, citing his past remarks that American Muslims are "ready to move to the next phase", and that within the next 15 years, the Muslim community "will have 50,000 - an army - of these people" who "will design [Islam's] image, protect the truth and the news [and] many of these people will run for public office, and they will become lawmakers". Abbott insisted Awad's intent is to "advance Sharia law". Awad previously told Middle East Eye that Abbott's move was a "stunt". Cair has long faced accusations that it is linked to the Muslim Brotherhood, but it maintains that its budget is overwhelmingly derived from donations by the American public, Muslim or otherwise. In a statement at the time of its designation in Texas, the organisation said that it has always denounced terrorism and antisemitism, and that Abbott's move was ultimately designed to curtail criticism of Israel. “Greg Abbott is an Israel First politician who has spent months stoking anti-Muslim hysteria to smear American Muslims critical of the Israeli government," Cair said. "By defaming another prominent American Muslim institution with debunked conspiracy theories and made-up quotes, Mr Abbott has once again shown that his top priority is advancing anti-Muslim bigotry, not serving the people of Texas. His latest publicity stunt has no basis in fact or law, nor can it stop our civil rights work." Wide assault One week ago, Cair was forced to shut down its operations in Florida after a judge declined to reverse the terrorist designation of the group there, which the state legislature and the governor had imposed. Cair shuts down Florida office as judge declines reversal of terrorist designation he Northern District of Florida acknowledged Florida's “novel - and perhaps unprecedented" new law allowing for terrorist designations of non-profit groups without due process, but ultimately said Cair's emergency request did not adequately prove that the group was suffering a criminal punishment. Winsor did, however, say Florida officials cannot prevent Cair from accessing legal services. Florida officials also pledged not to prosecute Cair's board, its staff, or its third-party associates. Cair has said it will now appeal the decision. In a statement, Cair's national deputy director, Edward Ahmed Mitchell, mourned the loss of its operations in the state. "For the first time in over twenty years, Florida Muslims cannot call their community’s leading civil rights organization for help if they experience a hate crime at their mosque, illegal discrimination in the workplace, violent bullying in school, or any other acts of bigotry." articles.summary: Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”. articles.body:
In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.

The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.

Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill.

That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable.

On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people.

Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work.

In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line.

After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity.

Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them.

“Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.”

He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard.

Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead.

Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market.

Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment.

His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”.

The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term.

The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have.

His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs.

So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR.”

articles.title: "Minacce russe non credibili, Ue non si faccia impressionare". Intervista a Gentiloni (VIDEO)
articles.summary: AGI - L’ Unione europea non dovrebbe farsi impressionare dalle "richieste impossibili o minacce improbabili" della Russia che paventa di “usare la forza contro l' Europa quando da cinque anni è impantanata in una guerra con l' Ucraina ”, una minaccia che “onestamente non è molto convincente". L'ex premier italiano e Commissario Ue Paolo Gentiloni , parlando con l'AGI a margine della seconda edizione del Lugano Global Forum , in corso nella città del Canton Ticino, spiega che i toni aggressivi e 'ultimativi' di Mosca nei confronti dell' Europa non lo colgono di sorpresa. "Non mi stupisce che la Russia abbia fatto filtrare la domanda di un arretramento della Nato nei confini che aveva alla fine del secolo scorso. Cose ridicole, ma che - osserva l'ex commissario Ue - fanno parte di una certa tradizione con la quale la Russia e, un tempo, l' Unione Sovietica , affrontano le dinamiche negoziali". La sostanza, osserva ancora Gentiloni , è infatti un'altra: "Mi sembra che comincia a farsi strada la possibilità di un negoziato e questo forse spiega anche questi toni ogni tanto estremi e minacciosi da parte russa ", conclude. Possibilità di negoziato e vertice trilaterale Parlando del primo vertice trilaterale dei leader di Usa , Cina e Russia , da giovedì a Shenzhen , Gentiloni ne sminuisce la portata, reale e potenziale: "Non mi aspetto grandi cose da questo incontro, che Putin ha fortemente voluto in Cina , perché al di là della 'photo opportunity' non credo che ci sarà sostanza". In vista dello storico trilaterale, Paolo Gentiloni afferma che "chi addirittura parla di una 'nuova Yalta' forse non ha capito in che mondo ci troviamo". In quanto alla possibilità che il vertice possa addirittura ridiscutere gli assetti della sicurezza europea , il giudizio è ancora più netto: ”È uno scenario ridicolo". Europa ai negoziati di pace Analizzando poi lo scenario che vedrebbe l' Ue, nel formato E-5 , al tavolo dei negoziati di pace tra Mosca e Kiev , Gentiloni spiega che "è ovvio che, se si andasse verso un negoziato, l' Europa ne farà parte". Interpellato a margine del Lugano Global Forum , quest'anno dedicato alle grandi sfide di un mondo in pieno sconvolgimento, l'ex premier e Commissario Ue sottolinea che "purtroppo finora ci sono stati incontri, qualche volta promossi da Erdogan , altre volte dai Paesi del Golfo , talvolta addirittura mediazioni promosse dal Santo Padre , che hanno avuto utili conseguenze umanitarie, per esempio sugli scambi di prigionieri, ma non hanno mai affrontato neanche lontanamente la questione della pace e del futuro dei rapporti tra Ucraina e Russia ". "Stiamo andando verso l'apertura di questo tipo di negoziato? Io non lo escludo, tuttavia - osserva - non è detto che Putin abbia accettato ", la presenza Ue al tavolo. "Può darsi che continui invece a sperare in un prolungamento della guerra o nella vittoria di Marine Le Pen . Alcuni segnali fanno pensare. L' Europa è per il sostegno all' Ucraina , l' Ucraina è in Europa e ovviamente se si arrivasse a un vero negoziato - rileva Gentiloni - l' Europa ne farà parte". Il formato della rappresentanza europea Parlando poi del formato con cui il Consiglio europeo ha deciso di partecipare, per Gentiloni “è tutt'altro che ideale” perché, dice, “sette persone sono tante, anche se sono probabilmente più esperte e più credibili di altre che saranno attorno a quel tavolo". Oltre alla presidente della Commissione europea e al presidente del Consiglio europeo , in caso di colloqui di pace con Kiev parteciperanno anche Germania , Francia , Italia , Polonia e Regno Unito nel caso di colloqui di pace con Kiev . Il fatto che l' Ue , anche in questo contesto, non sarà presente con un solo rappresentante, come auspicato da Mosca , "non è una novità", osserva Gentiloni , "anche in occasione di precedenti negoziati, pensiamo ai negoziati sul nucleare con l'Iran , gli europei comunque erano forse non 7 ma 4-5". Sostanzialmente, prosegue, "c'è una storica contraddizione tra una logica dell' Unione europea , che potrebbe portare ad avere un solo rappresentante, e la logica dei governi che vogliono tutti far parte delle delegazioni". La risposta a Calenda A chi, come il leader di Azione Carlo Calenda , sta accusando Bruxelles di essersi fatta "un clamoroso autogol" per non aver delegato un negoziatore unico a rappresentare l' Europa , Gentiloni risponde che "non è un autogol: è quello che vogliono i governi nazionali che poi, magari, contemporaneamente si lamentano di una delegazione troppo numerosa". Gentiloni preferisce infatti fermarsi alla sostanza delle cose: "Se il negoziato si aprisse, ovviamente l' Europa ne farebbe parte e con questo potrebbe essere finalmente imboccata la strada per terminare un conflitto che ormai dura da quasi cinque anni", conclude. Centrosinistra e sostegno all'Ucraina Parlando infine della situazione politica italiana, del centrosinistra in particolare, Gentiloni , che nel 2019 è stato anche presidente del Pd , spera che Elly Schlein e Giuseppe Conte troveranno una sintesi sull' Ucraina , al tavolo programmatico del centrosinistra . "Non partecipo a questa discussione ma mi auguro che trovino una sintesi", dice Paolo Gentiloni a margine del Lugano Global Forum . "La lingua italiana consente di trovare sintesi finché si è all'opposizione. Il problema - avverte ancora Gentiloni - è poi quando si va al governo". "Se il centrosinistra vince le elezioni, cosa che mi auguro, non potrà che continuare a sostenere l' Ucraina ”, conclude.

articles.title: Nvidia scandal: China's chips dilemma, US rivalry shape AI race
articles.summary: The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.
articles.preview: November 16, 2026 The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China. China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.
articles.body:
November 16, 2026

The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.

China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.

Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology, has been tasked with strengthening China's capacity for technological innovation, which would enhance its strategic competitiveness against the United States.

The party is currently using AI to monitor citizens, develop advanced unmanned weapons systems, and transform economic sectors through robotics and industrial automation, among other things.

But the US has so far been leading the way in manufacturing technology and chip design. And Washington has taken a slew of measures to retain its dominance in this strategic sector.

US moves to restrict China's access to chips

As early as 2023, the then Biden administration decided to restrict the export of advanced semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment to China, citing national security reasons.

Beijing slammed the US restrictions, calling them "unilateral and arbitrary."

US chipmakers, however, have been drawn to China's vast and rapidly growing market.

Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO of the American AI chip manufacturer Nvidia last week, enjoyed something of a rock star status in China. The 63-year-old, who was born in Taiwan, is viewed in China as a successful entrepreneur.

Huang, who has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trumpduring his second term, has pushed for looser regulations and fewer restrictions on selling AI chips to China.

In December, the Trump administration granted Nvidia permission to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the US got a 25% cut of sales.

Although the H200 is not part of Nvidia's highest-performance series, it is significantly more efficient than competing Chinese products.

Each of these chips carries a hefty $27,000 (€24,000) price tag, and Nvidia estimates demand in China at 2 million units, which corresponds to sales of approximately $5.4 billion from this product alone.

Nvidia affair and espionage allegations

But Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing.

The scandal not only sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industries, but also fueled highly contentious political debates in China and the US.

Washington, which sees its national security threatened, is said to be planning further restrictions against China to close loopholes that allow Chinese firms to acquire advanced American semiconductors.

China, on the other hand, denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Beijing also stepped up its rhetoric ahead of the meeting between President Xi Jinping and Trump at this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13.

Some Chinese media outlets have also criticized the reporting on the issue.

"Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?" asked China's state-run Global Times newspaper in an editorial.

It accused the US media of turning the affair into a "Hollywood thriller" but without providing the "hard evidence to back up the central allegations."

Many Chinese have also taken to the microblogging and social media platform Weibo to comment on the controversy.

A user wrote that Huang's downfall was, in essence, "the result of political maneuvering within the United States," while another user asked: "Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn't this plot a little too melodramatic?"

Behind the verbal sparring lies an economic calculation.

Is China buying more US chips?

Ding, the Chinese vice premier, has to decide whether China should continue to rely on US chips or back its domestic industry in the hope that it can achieve the breakthrough needed to surpass American competitors.

Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips, for instance, are currently sitting in Hong Kong, awaiting Chinese import approval.

The White House has already given the green light, but Beijing has yet to approve the imports.

For Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, that is puzzling. "To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term."

Chinese AI products are also increasingly using "Made in China" chips.

"This effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors," wrote Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology in a recent study on China's semiconductor strategy.

This is the case not only to civilian sectors. "Against the backdrop of the current complex geopolitical situation, strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure has become a core element of the national security strategy," Wang explained.

According to her, for example, the radar systems in China's fifth-generation Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and in the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile are equipped exclusively with Chinese chips.

China is increasingly focused on autonomous AI chip platforms developed domestically, Wang underscored.

"This has created a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia," she added.

China lacks advanced chip-making equipment

However, China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips.

Chip manufacturing requires lithography systems that expose raw silicon materials to ultraviolet light.

Bowing to pressure from Washington, the Dutch maker of lithography machines, ASML, has stopped exporting its most advanced machines to China.

The ban helps secure the US's technological lead in AI chips, said the Center for Technology & Statecraft, a Washington-based think tank. If China were to import additional ASML systems like it did in 2024 and 2025, "its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it."

According to the international consulting firm Deloitte, China is planning further extensive investments. "The focus is on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies."

Policymakers aim to stabilize the entire supply chain, expand self-sufficiency, and actively manage risks, the study noted. "The focus is shifting from supporting individual companies to fostering synergies within the supply chain, establishing quality systems, and ensuring the secure management of critical resources in order to promote the development of a more resilient industrial organizational structure."

This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Congo struggles to tame ebola outbreak six months into response
articles.summary: More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016
articles.preview: More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016
articles.body:
Ebola virus

Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.

More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities’ ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.

By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.

New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.

Questions over funding and management

Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.

One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.

Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.

Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.

“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF.

Children face high death rates

Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say.

Most children affected by the disease have not received specialized care, contributing to high death rates.

According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through Nov. 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died.

Conflict and attacks hamper response

Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices.

Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack.

The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict.

Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians.

The virus’s rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.

articles.title: DR Congo-Rwanda tensions force Francophonie leadership election delay until 2027
articles.summary: A diplomatic row between DR Congo and Rwanda has forced a major French-speaking nations summit to postpone its leadership election.
articles.preview: OIF A diplomatic dispute between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) and Rwanda has forced a major summit of French-speaking nations to postpone the election of a new leader until the end of 2027. The International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF) had been expected to elect its secretary-general during the summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. However, tensions escalated after DR Congo threatened to withdraw from the organisation if Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo secured a third term.
articles.body:
OIF

A diplomatic dispute between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) and Rwanda has forced a major summit of French-speaking nations to postpone the election of a new leader until the end of 2027.

The International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF) had been expected to elect its secretary-general during the summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. However, tensions escalated after DR Congo threatened to withdraw from the organisation if Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo secured a third term.

Speaking after the decision, Mushikiwabo acknowledged facing intense pressure but said she had maintained her candidacy because of her ambition to continue serving the organisation and her commitment to its reforms.

She said member states had agreed to postpone the election in the absence of consensus.

Tensions between the two African neighbours remain high, with Kinshasa accusing Kigali of supporting the M23 armed group, which has seized large areas of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies the allegations.

DR Congo’s potential departure would be a significant setback for the OIF. The country is home to millions of French speakers and is the organisation’s second-largest Francophone nation after France.

Mushikiwabo has confirmed she intends to remain a candidate when the election takes place at the end of 2027.

articles.title: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
articles.summary: Iran reports tanker mine strikes as a drone alert in Iraq and the arrival of a US aircraft carrier raise tensions.
articles.preview: Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region. Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict.
articles.body:
Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.

Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday that two oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised.

Separately, Iran’s regular navy said another tanker had caught fire and become immobilised after striking a mine in restricted waters east of the strait.

The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday.

In the latest incident, a tanker was disabled and an engine room fire broke out following an attack seven nautical miles (13km) north of Khasab, Oman.

Earlier, the maritime monitoring agency said another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported.

It remained unclear whether either incident was connected to the mine strikes claimed by Iran.

The incidents followed a series of attacks on commercial vessels in recent weeks. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone.

Drone alert at Iraq gas field

The threats to maritime energy shipments came as another security alert raised concerns over energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region.

In Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field on Monday, Reuters reported, citing two security sources.

There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage from the latest incident.

Production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week following a suspected drone attack that sparked a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to United Arab Emirates-based Dana Gas, one of the facility’s operators.

The field is a major source of natural gas for electricity generation in the Kurdish region, making disruptions particularly significant for local power supplies.

It has faced repeated attacks that Iraqi Kurdish officials have blamed on Iranian-backed armed groups.

No group was identified as responsible for Monday’s drone overflight.

The developments came as the US reinforced its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.

A US official confirmed its arrival to Al Jazeera on Monday, bringing the number of American aircraft carriers operating in the US Central Command area to three, as tensions with Iran remained high and diplomatic efforts to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained stalled.

articles.body:
Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.

But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.

Theonila Roka Matbob, a former cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.

Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.

“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.

“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.

“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”

The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.

The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.

The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

articles.title: Irish court jails man for life over Dublin knife attack that sparked riots
articles.summary: Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023.
articles.preview: Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023. A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life behind bars for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin on November 23, 2023, in an attack that triggered rioting and looting in the Irish capital. articles.body:
Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023.

A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life behind bars for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin on November 23, 2023, in an attack that triggered rioting and looting in the Irish capital.

Riad Bouchaker, an Algerian national and Irish citizen, was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court in Dublin on Monday after being found guilty in July on eight charges arising from the knife attack outside a school nearly three years ago.

His victims included a five-year-old girl, a six-year-old girl, a five-year-old boy and a woman in her mid-30s.

The youngest girl was stabbed in the heart, resulting in severe disability after her brain was deprived of oxygen for 40 minutes following the attack.

The girl, who is now eight, cannot speak and communicates only by blinking. She uses a wheelchair and is fed through a tube in her stomach because she is unable to swallow safely.

Bouchaker was also found guilty of assaulting childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious injuries as she tried to protect the children.

Speaking outside the court, Garda Superintendent Colm Murphy, the senior investigating officer, acknowledged the actions of those who intervened, the Press Association reported.

“I just want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the actions of those that immediately reacted to the situation as it unfolded, in particular to Leanne Flynn, who undoubtedly her actions on the day saved lives,” he said.

Within hours of the attack, false information about the suspect’s identity spread online, fuelling anger among anti-immigration activists and far-right groups.

The worst rioting seen in the Irish capital for decades erupted in the city centre as crowds clashed with police, set vehicles on fire and looted shops.

The violence shocked the country and triggered days of debate over immigration, online misinformation and public order.

Nearly 100 people were arrested, and more than 80 were charged with offences.

Bouchaker had pleaded not guilty to three counts of attempted murder and three counts of assault causing harm.

He also denied one count each of intentionally or recklessly causing serious harm and brandishing a dangerous weapon, a kitchen knife.

Judge Tony Hunt told the jury that two years before the attack, Bouchaker had suffered from a benign brain tumour that required surgery.

Hunt also said that due to interventions by bystanders immediately after the attack, Bouchaker suffered a head injury that required hospital treatment.

He was found fit to stand trial, and “there is no suggestion that he was suffering mental disorder at the time of the incident”, the judge said.

Evidence was heard from more than 80 witnesses, including eyewitnesses, emergency responders, police and forensic experts.

articles.body:
A police raid has failed to locate three Melbourne Cup trophies belonging to champion horse Makybe Diva after a smash and grab at Flemington racecourse.

A Mount Waverley home in Melbourne’s east was raided on Monday evening after thieves smashed their way into a glass display case at the racecourse about 6.30am.

A 36-year-old Malvern East man was arrested at the Solomon Street home.

He was interviewed by police and released, pending summons.

The trophies, which Victoria police says are valued at $1m each, are yet to be recovered.

The cups, won by the history-making mare in 2003, 2004 and 2005, had been on public display at the racecourse, which hosts the Melbourne Cup, since September.

The champion racehorse, which died in February at the age of 27 after a short and sudden battle with a gastrointestinal condition, was “the people’s horse’, former owner Tony Santic told 3AW.

“Hopefully we can get them back in one piece,” Santic said. “It’s more than devastating. I just can’t believe it.

“I just want to try to get them back and hopefully we get them back in one piece.”

The Victorian Racing Club said the theft was devastating.

“Victoria police is investigating a theft incident that occurred at Flemington racecourse [on Monday] morning involving three Melbourne Cup trophies,” it said.

“We are devastated by the incident and are in direct contact with Tony Santic.”

articles.body:
A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.

The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.

The George HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.

In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.

The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.

The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.

Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.

Last week, Trump warned Iran that the US military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.

“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.

Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.

Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.

Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.

In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.

Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.

Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.

Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.

Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.

US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade.

Independent assessments from Lloyd’s List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels.

articles.body:
Una nuova mail bombing è arrivata nella tarda mattinata alle scuole di varie città italiane. "Ho appena ricevuto l'incarico di piazzare e attivare un ordigno esplosivo nel vostro edificio - si legge nel messaggio di posta elettronico firmato M.A., iniziali di Mikhail Andropov firma comparsa nelle mail simili arrivate nei giorni scorsi - L'esplosione avverrà tra 40 minuti". I presidi stavolta si sono attenuti alle nuove direttive del Viminale e nessun istituto è stato evacuato. Il mittente delle email sarebbe riconducibile ad un unico indirizzo che rimanda al Dipartimento per gli affari accademici e l'assicurazione della qualità dell'Università vietnamita di Da Nang, in Vietnam. Si tratta del terzo caso in pochi giorni e come nei casi precedenti è ipotizzabile che l'account sia stato hackerato.

Le indagini della Polizia Postale sono in corso e andrà capito se, come già nei precedenti casi, la mail provenga appunto da un indirizzo hackerato o se sia stata usata una VPN che nasconde l'indirizzo di provenienza. In base alle nuove linee guida, di fronte a mail seriali e prive di riscontri oggettivi, non scatta più l'evacuazione automatica degli edifici ma le segnalazioni vengono subito prese in carico dalle questure e dalla Polizia Postale. L'email in questione conteneva una novità rispetto alle due dei giorni scorsi, ovvero un riferimento anche alle mense scolastiche. Tuttavia il fatto non ha colto impreparati i dirigenti scolastici che si sono attenuti alle nuove disposizioni e non hanno perso la calma. Solo in pochi casi c'è stata una interruzione precauzionale del servizio mensa che poi, dopo i controlli, è ripreso regolarmente. Nella email si legge infatti anche: "Abbiamo reclutato un dipendente della vostra mensa, che ha mescolato al cibo e alle provviste una miscela tossica a base di azoturo di sodio e cianuro di potassio". "E' l'ennesima email con messaggi farneticanti e grotteschi - ha detto all'ANSA il presidente dei presidi di ANP, Antonello Giannelli - Sono contenuti che vanno ignorati e girati alla polizia postale e così hanno fatto i colleghi". Tra gli istituti romani ai quali è stata recapitata l'email e che ha sospeso, precauzionalmente, il servizio mensa, c'è l'istituto comprensivo Hypatia a Tor Bella Monaca, che conta 940 allievi. Ma, come ha spiegato la dirigente, Annalisa Laudando all'ANSA, una volta effettuati i controlli, tutti gli alunni hanno regolarmente pranzato. Sulla vicenda è intervenuto anche il ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani, il quale ha spiegato che in Europa si lavorerà sempre di più insieme contro gli attachi hacker. "In Italia è stato respinto quest'altro attacco di spam di mail, nessuna scuola è stata chiusa perché si trattava di una falsa minaccia. Però l'obiettivo era quello di continuare a provocare caos", ha detto. Prosegue intanto l'ondata di occupazioni di istituti in tutta Italia. Mentre alcuni studenti 'disoccupano', consentendo la ripresa delle lezioni, altri istituti superiori vengono occupati da nord a sud. Gli studenti lamentano mancanza di investimenti per la scuola, risorse buttate per le armi e angoscia per il futuro.
