November 16, 2026

Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.

"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.

Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.

Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.

The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.

"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.

"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."

She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.

Turkey as a stopover

"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."

Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.

Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.

According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.

A US naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.

The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.

The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.

The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.

She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.

"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."

Young Iranians lose faith in the future

The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.

A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.

The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.

Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.

Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.

Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.

"That's my dream of a better future," he said.

This article was originally published in German.

articles.body:
news

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on Sunday threatened to take action against drugs at "the source" amid longstanding accusations by Algiers that neighbouring Morocco was behind drug trafficking into the country.

Tebboune did not name Morocco in an address at the Algerian Supreme Court, but Algiers has often blamed Morocco as being the source of drugs trafficked through their shared border. "It's a war declared against Algeria, and when there's war the army is of course at the front line," Tebboune said. "If necessary, we can go further, even to the source of the drugs' production, in legitimate self-defence."

On Thursday, authorities said they destroyed nearly 10 tonnes of recently seized cannabis resin as well as 33 million psychotropic pills, although it remained unclear where the drugs had come from. Relations between Algeria and Morocco have been tense since Algiers severed diplomatic ties in 2021.

Last month, Tebboune also said drug trafficking into Algeria was part of a "hybrid war" waged by "saboteurs", although he again did not name any actors. The Algerian defence ministry regularly announces confiscating large amounts of drugs, with statements often saying they came from Morocco.

articles.title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
articles.summary: Russia said Ukraine had launched over 2,000 drones over the course of a day, while Kyiv came under a record 17 air raid alerts.
articles.preview: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit. The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added. Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day.
articles.body:
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.

Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.

The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.

The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.

Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.

Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.

The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.

A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.

But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.

"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title: Come è nata la falsa notizia del blackout globale del 17 novembre
articles.summary: È un allarme privo di prove che fa leva sulla preoccupazione dei recenti attacchi informatici
articles.preview: Sono giorni che, sui social media, circolano post in cui si avverte di un possibile blackout mondiale che si dovrebbe verificare martedì 17 novembre. Questi contenuti allarmistici non spiegano mai bene le cause del blackout, ma descrivono uno scenario in cui le città saranno paralizzate e la popolazione resterà al buio, senza elettricità, senza Internet, con conti bancari bloccati e trasporti pubblici inaccessibili per 72 ore. Le persone vengono quindi fortemente invitate a fare scorte di contanti, acqua ed alimenti non deperibili.
articles.body:
Sono giorni che, sui social media, circolano post in cui si avverte di un possibile blackout mondiale che si dovrebbe verificare martedì 17 novembre. Questi contenuti allarmistici non spiegano mai bene le cause del blackout, ma descrivono uno scenario in cui le città saranno paralizzate e la popolazione resterà al buio, senza elettricità, senza Internet, con conti bancari bloccati e trasporti pubblici inaccessibili per 72 ore. Le persone vengono quindi fortemente invitate a fare scorte di contanti, acqua ed alimenti non deperibili.

Un allarme che fa leva sulla preoccupazione degli attacchi informatici delle scorse settimane in diversi Paesi europei, dei (falsi) allarmi bomba negli aeroporti e nelle scuole, e del problema informatico che ha bloccato per diversi tempo i servizi di Microsoft.

Ma di questo blackout del 17 novembre, non esistono prove. Questa storia, del tutto infondata, è nata travisando alcuni eventi recenti reali. Il primo riguarda le nuove linee guida della Commissione europea, presentate lo scorso 3 novembre al Forum europeo sulla protezione civile, per aiutare le persone a prepararsi alle emergenze ed essere autosufficienti per 72 ore, durante i primi giorni di un’eventuale crisi. Le linee guida arrivano a seguito dell’approvazione a marzo 2025 della Strategia dell’Unione europea in materia di preparazione. La Commissione ha proposto anche l’istituzione di una Giornata europea della preparazione alle emergenze, ma a partire dal prossimo anno, il 2027, e il 23 ottobre (non il 17 novembre). Da tempo documenti delle istituzioni europee o frasi dei suoi rappresentanti vengono manipolati in rete per diffondere tesi complottistiche di vario genere.

La data del 17 novembre ipotizzata dai contenuti social allarmistici arriva invece dagli Stati Uniti. Nel Paese, infatti, martedì le emittenti radiofoniche e televisive interromperanno la normale programmazione per trasmettere un messaggio di prova. Si tratta di un test triennale per verificare la funzionalità del sistema di allarme in caso di una reale emergenza nazionale. A svolgerlo sarà l’Ente federale per la gestione delle emergenze (FEMA), e ne aveva dato annuncio lo scorso settembre la Commissione federale per le comunicazioni (FCC).

Secondo poi diversi post questo fantomatico blackout globale del 17 novembre sarebbe stato profetizzato dai Simpson. Un episodio della serie televisiva statunitense – a cui sono stati attribuiti poteri divinatori per alcune coincidenze con la realtà – avrebbe infatti rivelato questa data di un prossimo blackout. Si tratta del settimo episodio della 35ª stagione, andato in onda originariamente il 19 novembre 2023 e intitolato “It’s a Blunderful Life”, in cui una Lisa Simpson adulta ripensa a un’interruzione di corrente che lasciò Springfield al buio per sei giorni, avvenuta proprio il 17 novembre.

Tuttavia, nell’episodio non viene specificato l’anno del blackout, e l’interruzione di corrente – della durata di sei giorni – termina il Giorno del Ringraziamento. Nel 2026 però questa festività cade il 26 novembre, ovvero 9 giorni più tardi la data del blackout ipotizzato. Inoltre, nell’episodio il blackout colpisce solo la cittadina di Springfield e non tutto il pianeta. Anche questo caso rientra quindi nel filone disinformativo che attribuisce ai Simpson poteri divinatori a causa di alcune coincidenze occorse nelle oltre 700 puntate andate in onda.

articles.title: Scattered by war, the band that gave voice to Sudan's revolution plays again
articles.summary: The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered his 'Aswat al-Madina' (Arabic for Voices of the City) band across continents
articles.preview: The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered his 'Aswat al-Madina' (Arabic for Voices of the City) band across continents
articles.body:
Sudan

The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered them across multiple continents.

After living through revolution, war and years of displacement, Mustafa and his fellow musicians in "Aswat al-Madina" (Arabic for Voices of the City) have reunited in the Egyptian capital, returning to both recording and live performance.

"I still can't quite process the fact that we're back together," said Mustafa, the band's guitarist and co-founder, who goes by Timon.

"It still feels unreal," he told AFP between recording takes, as back home war rages between the two forces Sudan's youth once rallied against: the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

In the studio, old stories and songs transport the musicians back to Khartoum, where they became the soundtrack to Sudan's 2018 uprising against longtime ruler Omar al-Bashir.

Two days before war erupted between the army and the RSF, former allies who worked together to derail Sudan's transition to democracy, the band was debating setlists for their next performance.

Instead, they found themselves swept up in the conflict, which has since devastated Sudan, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing millions more.

'Never left me'

Founded in Khartoum in 2014, Aswat al-Madina was part of a wave of underground bands pushing Sudanese music beyond conventional boundaries.

Blending folk traditions with jazz, reggae and contemporary rhythms, they sang about corruption, social injustice and life under authoritarian rule.

"Before the revolution, we used a technique where everyone understood what we meant, but nobody could prove it," said lead singer Ibrahim Ahmed Taha, who was arrested several times over their music.

When Sudan's youth took to the streets in December 2018, demanding an end to Bashir's rule, the band's songs blasted from phones, passing cars and makeshift barricades.

Timon still remembers one demonstrator carrying a giant speaker blaring their music through the marches.

"The music pushed people forward. It told them not to retreat in the face of repression.

"That image has never left me."

The band was a regular fixture at pro-democracy protests, including at the sit-in outside military headquarters in Khartoum, where protesters gathered each evening to listen to speeches, poetry and music.

"Find me in the square at half-past revolution; tonight, the devil falls," one track goes.

That sit-in became the site of a massacre in June 2019, when security forces led by the military and the RSF killed at least 120 protesters.

Four years later, when those same forces turned their guns on each other, the band -- like many Sudanese - lost everything.

From their five-storey creative hub, "everything was gone," Timon said.

"Not just the musical equipment. Even the chairs and tables had been looted."

"You'd step into the street and see bodies lying there and buildings reduced to rubble. That's when you realise everything has fallen apart," Timon said.

As fighting spread, the musicians fled Sudan, carrying little more than backpacks and laptops.

'In Khartoum again'

Timon escaped to the United Arab Emirates while others settled in Egypt and elsewhere in Africa. Regular rehearsals gave way to anxious discussions of visas and relatives still trapped in Sudan.

It was only this August that the band could reunite in Cairo, for its first performance since the war began.

As familiar songs filled the venue, audience members sang along to every word, shouting requests.

"For a moment," Taha said, "I felt like I was in Khartoum again."

For keyboard player Roba Bashir, the band's only woman member, the reunion was "the happiest day since the war began".

Musab Mahgoub, who has attended two of the band's Cairo concerts since August, said the performances "brought back so many old memories of Sudan".

The band now hopes to tour internationally and is recording a new version of their song "Nos Kobayet Shai Bi'Aisha" ("Half a Cup of Tea with Bread") with an Egyptian-Nubian collaborator, its themes of home and family taking on special meaning in exile.

articles.title: Sudan and Ethiopia trade accusations over armed groups
articles.summary: Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighboring African countries.
articles.preview: Sudan Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighbouring African countries. Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks.
articles.body:
Sudan

Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighbouring African countries.

Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks.

In early November, the Sudanese military filed complaints against Ethiopia with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, saying it submitted evidence to back up its case. Within days, Ethiopia expelled six staff members of a Sudanese Consulate and ordered the mission closed.

Ethiopia says the Sudanese military supports rebels fighting Ethiopian federal forces in its Tigray border region, where fighting returned in September, shattering a 2022 peace agreement.

Each country denies the other's accusations, and The Associated Press could not independently verify their claims. But the tensions — compounded by competing regional alliances and contentious issues over resources and disputed territory — risk a wider regional conflict.

Jervin Naidoo, a senior political economist at Oxford Economics Africa, told the AP that the situation “raises the risk that instability inside Ethiopia becomes another front in Sudan’s war — and vice versa.”

Here’s a closer look at what's behind the escalation and how it could impact the wider region:

Sudan’s military says Ethiopia backs Sudanese paramilitary forces

Sudan was plunged into war in April 2023, when long-simmering tensions between the army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, turned into all-out fighting.

So far, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or ACLED, a conflict monitor, though aid groups warn that the real number is likely much higher. Some 13 million people have been displaced.

The war, now in its fourth year, has left the Sudanese military in control of the north, east and central regions, including Sudan’s Red Sea ports and its oil refineries and pipelines. The RSF and its allies control western Darfur and parts of Kordofan along the border with South Sudan — both regions rich in oil fields and gold mines.

The latest flashpoint in the war is in Sudan's Blue Nile province, which borders Ethiopia.

In late August, the Humanitarian Research Lab, a Yale University research group that uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts, found an increase in military vehicles and equipment at an Ethiopian military base in Asosa, a city near the Sudanese border.

Based on satellite imagery, the Yale group confirmed the buildup was linked to the RSF.

“The RSF is engaged out of Ethiopia ... to try to open a second front,” said Nathaniel Raymond, head of the research group.

Ethiopia says Sudan’s military backs the Tigray rebels

Fighting resumed in September in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, where the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, and Ethiopian federal troops fought between 2020 and 2022, when a peace deal was signed.

Later that month, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, suggested that Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt were supporting rebel troops who at the time had captured several strategic towns. The allegations drew sharp denials from the three neighbours.

In early November, Ethiopia expelled the six staff members of Sudan’s mission in Asosa and closed the consulate.

Naidoo, from Oxford Economics Africa, warned that continued fighting in Tigray could divert Ethiopia’s attention from its myriad other issues and increase the risk of weapons and fighters flowing across the border with Sudan.

“All the ingredients are present for an intensifying proxy war between Ethiopia and Sudan that further destabilises both countries,” said Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa project director at the International Crisis Group.

Unresolved disputes, competing political alliances and a flashpoint border

Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated since late last year, when the RSF established camps on Ethiopian territory, according to Ladd Serwat, senior Africa analyst at ACLED.

In October, a drone strike blamed on the RSF hit a gathering of displaced people on Sudan's border with Ethiopia and killed 41, said the Emergency Lawyers rights group, which tracks the war in Sudan.

“Sudan and Ethiopia don’t operate in a vacuum; their relations amid these current domestic conflicts are shaped by external backers,” said Serwat, adding that Ethiopia is allied with the United Arab Emirates while Sudan is part of an Egypt-Eritrea regional alliance.

Turkey has been balancing, backing both Khartoum and Addis Ababa, he said.

Serwat added that Ethiopia’s support for the RSF is primarily logistical, while the UAE remains its main backer, funding camps and supplying weapons. The UAE has repeatedly denied any involvement in Sudan’s war.

Other issues have also marred relations, including Ethiopia's construction of a huge dam — Africa’s largest dam — on the Blue Nile, the main Nile River tributary. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam near the Ethiopia-Sudan border cost about $5 billion and was completed in 2025, aiming to boost Ethiopia's power production and economy.

But it has triggered a dispute with Egypt and Sudan, which have called for a legally binding agreement on the dam’s filling and operation to protect their own water resources.

Another issue is the disputed border region of Al-Fashaga, where Ethiopian farmers have long cultivated the area's fertile soil, according to the International Crisis Group. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved in to reassert control over the area as Ethiopian troops were distracted fighting with the Tigray rebels.

The Sudan-Ethiopia tensions may not have gained much attention, but if ignored, they could escalate further and lead to mass displacements of people, Raymond's Yale group said.

articles.title: Che cosa sta facendo l’Italia per difendersi dagli attacchi informatici
articles.summary: I numeri sono in aumento e negli ultimi anni sono state introdotte nuove regole e stanziate risorse per prevenire e contrastare le minacce. Ma capire quanto queste misure abbiano funzionato non è semplice
articles.preview: L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.
articles.body:
L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.

Questi episodi si inseriscono in un quadro che ha riportato l’attenzione sulle minacce informatiche e la capacità dell’Italia di contrastarle efficacemente. Il 7 novembre il ministero degli Esteri aveva reso nota la diffusione sul dark web di dati personali del ministro Antonio Tajani. Il Ministro ha collegato le minacce alla posizione italiana sulla guerra in Ucraina e ha chiesto di affrontare il tema delle minacce ibride al G7 degli Esteri, che si è svolto a Parigi il 9 e 10 novembre. Un altro episodio era stato registrato a inizio novembre, quando alcuni supermercati italiani erano stati colpiti da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione, sui cui il governo aveva fatto il punto in una riunione il 3 novembre.

Il 9 novembre il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto, in un’intervista al Corriere della Sera, ha definito la guerra ibrida una «sfida epocale», che deve essere affrontata tramite una strategia comune tra le istituzioni. Una posizione in linea con quanto detto qualche giorno dalla presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni, che aveva richiamato l’attenzione sui possibili effetti degli attacchi informatici, sottolineando i rischi per le infrastrutture civili.

Negli ultimi anni, l’Italia ha introdotto nuove regole, istituito strutture dedicate alla cybersicurezza e stanziato risorse per proteggere le proprie infrastrutture digitali. Ma quali interventi sono stati realizzati e che cosa dicono i dati disponibili sulla loro efficacia?

articles.summary: Three months since introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corba has raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
articles.preview: Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue. The startup came out of stealth in August.
articles.body:
Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.

David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.

At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg.

David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”

SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.

More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

articles.title: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access ‘company information’
articles.summary: The cybersecurity and automation giant said it's working with outside investigators to understand the scale of the breach.
articles.preview: Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors. Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.
articles.body:
Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors.

Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.”

“We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.”

TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch.

One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach.

According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents.

Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor.

The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach.

Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands.

articles.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
articles.summary: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Nvidia should answer.
articles.preview: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang. Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
articles.body:
Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.

For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.

Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.

Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.

Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.

Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.

An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.

So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.

China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.

But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.

Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.

So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.

China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.

The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.

Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.

Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

articles.title: California files lawsuit against OpenAI alleging lack of proper safeguards
articles.summary: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was 'entirely predictable' result of emphasis on rapid growth.
articles.preview: Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth. California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards. The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.
articles.body:
Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth.

California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.

The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.

It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face.

In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.

The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.

“The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads.

The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government.

President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth.

In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development.

“United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative,” the order reads.

“My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standard — not 50 discordant State ones.”

Polls, however, show that a majority of Americans want to see greater oversight of AI development and are wary that the technology could fuel economic and social disruptions.

The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, for instance, found in October that 64 percent of US adults believe AI is developing too rapidly. Roughly 81 percent said the technology should be kept under human control, rather than be left to operate independently.

Several high-profile resignations in the AI sector — notably that of Jacob Coxon in September — have also spurred concerns about the lack of oversight.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon, formerly a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic, wrote in a social media post about his departure.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

In Monday’s lawsuit, California officials accuse companies like OpenAI of failing to “adequately secure and monitor” their AI tests. It also alleged that the company had obstructed state investigators when they attempted to look into incidents like the Hugging Face hacking.

“OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.

OpenAI has responded to July’s incident by stating that it would reinforce its safety measures and acknowledging the need for greater transparency.

In September, it also published a framework for “tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment” to better inform lawmakers and the public.

articles.body:
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.

OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.

The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.

After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

articles.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. "I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer," Altman said today. "I think the home tinkering is great."
articles.preview: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. "I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer," Altman said today. "I think the home tinkering is great."
articles.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”

Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’

The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.

Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”

AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”

Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:

“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”

Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

articles.title: Google spegne il motore di ricerca alle scuole che rifiutano l’ia
articles.summary: Negli Stati Uniti chi vuole tenere l’intelligenza artificiale fuori dalle aule dovrà rinunciare anche al motore di ricerca. La scelta ha scatenato le proteste di genitori, insegnanti e politici
articles.preview: Il 3 novembre Google ha annunciato che dall’inizio del 2027 i suoi strumenti di intelligenza artificiale saranno disattivati per gli studenti delle scuole statunitensi, da quella dell’infanzia alle superiori, a meno che i dirigenti scolastici non decidano di attivarli. Sembra una concessione a chi chiede più controllo sul rapporto tra bambini e chatbot. Ma c’è un problema, spiega il New York Times: le scuole che rifiuteranno del tutto l’ia perderanno anche l’accesso a Google Search, il motore di ricerca dell’azienda.
articles.body:
Il 3 novembre Google ha annunciato che dall’inizio del 2027 i suoi strumenti di intelligenza artificiale saranno disattivati per gli studenti delle scuole statunitensi, da quella dell’infanzia alle superiori, a meno che i dirigenti scolastici non decidano di attivarli. Sembra una concessione a chi chiede più controllo sul rapporto tra bambini e chatbot.

Ma c’è un problema, spiega il New York Times: le scuole che rifiuteranno del tutto l’ia perderanno anche l’accesso a Google Search, il motore di ricerca dell’azienda. “La ricerca e l’ia sono profondamente integrate”, ha detto Chris Phillips, vicepresidente di Google per l’istruzione. Nelle scuole che hanno vietato l’ia, ha aggiunto, gli studenti non avranno accesso al motore di ricerca e vedranno un messaggio d’avviso che il servizio non è disponibile.

La decisione pesa particolarmente perché Google è ovunque nelle scuole statunitensi. I Chromebook, i computer portatili economici dell’azienda, sono i dispositivi più distribuiti agli studenti. Sull’Atlantic il giornalista Will Oremus li descrive come un “cavallo di Troia” dell’intelligenza artificiale nelle scuole.

Con un Chromebook scolastico basta aprire l’app Gemini per farsi scrivere un tema. Oppure si può digitare un problema di algebra nella barra di ricerca e ottenere la soluzione già pronta in un Ai Overview, il riassunto generato automaticamente dall’intelligenza artificiale in cima ai risultati.

Negli ultimi mesi la resistenza di genitori e insegnanti è cresciuta. A settembre i due distretti scolastici più grandi del paese, New York e Los Angeles, hanno limitato l’accesso degli studenti all’ia generativa sui dispositivi a scuola. La settimana prima dell’annuncio di Google, lo stato di New York ha approvato una legge sulla sicurezza dei chatbot che vieta alle aziende di offrire ai minori diverse funzioni dell’intelligenza artificiale.

Il sindaco di New York Zohran Mamdani ha scritto sui social media: “Nessuna azienda dovrebbe avere il potere di imporci come educare i nostri figli”. Lina Khan, ex presidente della Federal trade commission, l’autorità statunitense per la concorrenza, ha accusato Google di usare il suo “monopolio della ricerca sul web per costringere le scuole” ad adottare la sua intelligenza artificiale, Gemini.

Scelta automatica

Ad agosto Google aveva attivato per impostazione predefinita le funzioni di ia dentro Classroom, la piattaforma usata per assegnare i compiti. La novità valeva per gli studenti di tutte le età, nelle scuole che già consentivano l’accesso a Gemini. Alcuni dirigenti avevano protestato.

“Un distretto scolastico non dovrebbe adottare per sbaglio una piattaforma di ia solo perché sei mesi fa nessuno ha trovato la casella giusta da spuntare per la rinuncia”, aveva detto James O’Hagan, responsabile dell’innovazione di un distretto del Wisconsin. “La regola dovrebbe essere la scelta, non l’adozione automatica”. Ora Google ha fatto marcia indietro su quel meccanismo, ma sulla ricerca non cede.

L’azienda sostiene che le critiche nascano da un equivoco. “Gli annunci di oggi danno alle scuole più scelta, non meno”, ha scritto su X. È vero, osserva l’Atlantic: Google non ha mai offerto una versione della ricerca senza ia (c’è solo una scheda “Web” che mostra unicamente i link), e ora sia Gemini sia Search saranno spenti per impostazione predefinita, con la possibilità di attivarli.

Per le scuole che sceglieranno di riattivare il motore di ricerca ci saranno due opzioni. La prima include gli Ai Overviews e le chat con l’ia, come la versione per il pubblico. La seconda si basa su Guided learning, una funzione di Gemini che dovrebbe guidare lo studente passo dopo passo senza dargli le risposte.

Ma in un test del New York Times la versione per il pubblico di Guided learning ha prodotto un tema dettagliato su una traccia di storia. La versione scolastica, ancora in fase di sperimentazione, avrà più limiti: per esempio, gli insegnanti potranno leggere le conversazioni degli studenti con il chatbot.

Resta il fatto che Google non offre quello che le scuole chiedono di più: una ricerca tradizionale, senza risposte generate. Come vorrebbe il distretto di Los Angeles. Lo chiede anche Richard Culatta, amministratore delegato di Iste+Ascd, un’organizzazione non profit che promuove l’uso della tecnologia nelle scuole e che pure ha ricevuto finanziamenti da Google.

La logica dell’azienda, spiega l’Atlantic, è che in un certo senso tutta la ricerca è già basata sull’intelligenza artificiale: da anni Google usa modelli linguistici per ordinare i risultati. Ma genitori e insegnanti non contestano l’algoritmo che decide quali link mostrare. Contestano un motore di ricerca trasformato in una macchina che dà risposte istantanee, soggette a errori, e che abitua i ragazzi a delegare il pensiero critico e la valutazione delle fonti.

Dietro la linea di Google c’è anche una ragione commerciale. I chatbot sono la minaccia più seria mai affrontata dal motore di ricerca: la OpenAiI sostiene che ChatGptPT gestisce ormai un volume di ricerche pari a circa un quinto di quello di Google. E, secondo l’Atlantic, Google scommette che la comodità vincerà sui dubbi.

Intanto qualcuno cerca alternative: DuckDuckGo, un motore di ricerca attento alla privacy degli utenti, afferma che l’uso della sua opzione di ricerca senza ia è cresciuto del 30 per cento da settembre, e che sta studiando un modo per aiutare le scuole che rinunceranno a Google a cambiare il motore di ricerca predefinito.

Kelly Clancy, madre di un ragazzo che frequenta la seconda media in una scuola pubblica di New York, è alla guida di alcuni gruppi che chiedono una moratoria sull’ia nelle scuole. Racconta che il figlio usa Google ogni giorno per i compiti, come una recente ricerca di scienze sulla sicurezza in laboratorio. “Dobbiamo ripensare da zero il modo in cui insegniamo ai ragazzi a fare ricerca”, dice. Magari, suggerisce, tornando in biblioteca, o usando altri motori di ricerca che permettono di controllare meglio l’ia.

Secondo Morgan Polikoff, che insegna scienze dell’educazione alla University of Southern California, la scelta di Google potrebbe dare nuova forza al movimento di genitori e insegnanti contro la tecnologia a scuola: “È un esempio particolarmente chiaro di come l’industria tecnologica faccia di tutto per imporci l’ia, anche quando abbiamo detto che non la vogliamo”. ◆

Francesca Di Muro

articles.title: Le aziende costruttrici di data center non stanno andando bene
articles.summary: Il “Financial Times” ha scritto che la sfiducia verso l'intelligenza artificiale ha portato a un grosso calo in borsa del settore
articles.preview: Il “Financial Times” ha scritto che la sfiducia verso l'intelligenza artificiale ha portato a un grosso calo in borsa del settore Il quotidiano finanziario Financial Times ha scritto che il settore delle aziende legate alla costruzione di data center ha perso 4.200 miliardi di dollari di valore in borsa negli ultimi sei mesi. È quasi la metà dei 9.400 miliardi di valore che il settore aveva guadagnato nei 12 mesi precedenti.
articles.body:
Il “Financial Times” ha scritto che la sfiducia verso l'intelligenza artificiale ha portato a un grosso calo in borsa del settore

Il quotidiano finanziario Financial Times ha scritto che il settore delle aziende legate alla costruzione di data center ha perso 4.200 miliardi di dollari di valore in borsa negli ultimi sei mesi. È quasi la metà dei 9.400 miliardi di valore che il settore aveva guadagnato nei 12 mesi precedenti. Il Financial Times scrive che è un calo dovuto al fatto che «la fiducia degli investitori nel boom dell’intelligenza artificiale sta vacillando».

Le aziende di cui parla il Financial Times non sono quelle tecnologiche che si occupano di hardware e software per l’intelligenza artificiale, ma quelle che forniscono energia e materiali per la costruzione dei centri. Cita per esempio Caterpillar, uno dei principali fornitori di generatori a gas per i data center, l’azienda produttrice di energia nucleare Oklo, l’azienda che produce sistemi di raffreddamento Comfort Systems e quella di tecnologie ottiche Corning. Tutte, scrive il Financial Times, da giugno hanno perso più del 40 per cento del loro valore in borsa.

All’origine di tutto c’è l’enorme crescita del settore dell’intelligenza artificiale – e quindi dei data center – che fino a qualche mese fa aveva spinto gli investitori a comprare azioni di queste aziende in previsione di un continuo aumento dei cantieri. Negli ultimi mesi le cose però sono un po’ cambiate e molti hanno venduto quelle azioni, portando a un crollo del valore di mercato delle aziende.

I data center sono grossi stabilimenti industriali pieni di computer, server, cavi e infrastrutture digitali, di cui le aziende tecnologiche hanno bisogno per far funzionare i loro servizi. La loro costruzione è diventata urgente e fondamentale con lo sviluppo di modelli di intelligenza artificiale sempre più avanzati, che per funzionare richiedono data center sempre più performanti.

Ultimamente però i data center hanno cominciato ad avere una pessima reputazione. Negli Stati Uniti l’ostilità verso la loro costruzione è una delle poche cose che hanno messo d’accordo Democratici e Repubblicani alle ultime elezioni di metà mandato. Ma proteste contro le nuove costruzioni sono state organizzate anche in altri paesi negli ultimi mesi. Oltre a comportare cantieri enormi, i data center sono infatti spesso rumorosi e richiedono grandi quantità di energia, che viene così sottratta alle comunità vicine.

– Leggi anche: Le proteste contro i data center sono arrivate anche in Italia

Oltre a questo c’è la grande prudenza legata al timore che il settore delle AI si riveli una bolla, dal momento che finora si è basato su enormi investimenti che però non hanno ancora permesso alle aziende di guadagnare altrettanto. È a questo che ci si riferisce quando si parla di «sfiducia nel settore delle AI»: più si va avanti e più l’incertezza cresce. Recentemente per esempio è uscita la notizia che in Cina le aziende che sviluppano modelli di AI hanno subito pesanti perdite in borsa.

Tra gli esperti sentiti dal Financial Times c’è chi sostiene che il calo del valore di queste aziende in borsa non significhi che il settore della costruzione di data center abbia smesso di crescere e che questo sia dimostrato dalla quantità di ordini che le aziende continuano a ricevere; altri fanno notare invece come gli ordini non siano un indicatore rappresentativo, perché sono il risultato di valutazioni ormai vecchie e che potrebbero essere state superate.

Bisogna anche vedere se negli Stati Uniti cambierà qualcosa nella normativa, dal momento che la lotta ai data center è stato uno dei temi principali delle campagne di politici locali e nazionali che sono stati eletti alle ultime elezioni.

articles.title: Il caso Nvidia non è solo una storia di corna e spie: c’è il contrabbando
articles.summary: L'imprenditrice e forse spia Alice Huang faceva arrivare i chip in Cina, violando la legge? E il capo di Nvidia ne sapeva qualcosa?
articles.preview: L'imprenditrice e forse spia Alice Huang faceva arrivare i chip in Cina, violando la legge? E il capo di Nvidia ne sapeva qualcosa? Il dipartimento del Commercio degli Stati Uniti aveva cominciato a indagare sull’imprenditrice cinese Alice Huang nel 2024, ben prima che venisse fuori la sua relazione con l’ex CEO di Nvidia Jensen Huang, dimessosi giovedì, e ancora prima che si cominciasse a parlare di lei come di una possibile spia del governo cinese.
articles.body:
L'imprenditrice e forse spia Alice Huang faceva arrivare i chip in Cina, violando la legge? E il capo di Nvidia ne sapeva qualcosa?

Il dipartimento del Commercio degli Stati Uniti aveva cominciato a indagare sull’imprenditrice cinese Alice Huang nel 2024, ben prima che venisse fuori la sua relazione con l’ex CEO di Nvidia Jensen Huang, dimessosi giovedì, e ancora prima che si cominciasse a parlare di lei come di una possibile spia del governo cinese.

Il motivo è che Megaspeed, un’azienda di data center di Singapore fondata nel 2023 e di cui Alice Huang è stata dirigente, è sospettata di aver gestito il contrabbando di microchip di Nvidia, tra i più potenti al mondo per l’intelligenza artificiale, di cui gli Stati Uniti vietano l’esportazione in Cina dal 2022.

Alice Huang non sarebbe la prima: che microchip avanzati prodotti negli Stati Uniti arrivino in Cina di contrabbando aggirando i controlli sulle esportazioni è noto. Negli ultimi anni il dipartimento di Giustizia ha incriminato diverse persone per averli fatti passare illegalmente attraverso paesi del Sudest asiatico. Quello che rende questo caso eccezionale è l’eventuale ruolo che avrebbe avuto Jensen Huang, cittadino statunitense e capo di una delle più importanti aziende tecnologiche del paese.

Breve riassunto della vicenda: Nvidia ha il monopolio di fatto nella progettazione di GPU, chip avanzatissimi che negli ultimi anni si sono rivelati fondamentali per lo sviluppo dei sistemi di intelligenza artificiale. Negli Stati Uniti il blocco alle esportazioni di chip verso la Cina era stato imposto prima dall’amministrazione di Joe Biden e poi da quella di Donald Trump, con lo scopo di contrastare il progresso tecnologico cinese.

Per Nvidia questo aveva comportato molti mancati guadagni, e infatti Jensen Huang aveva provato a lungo a convincere Trump a modificare le norme sull’esportazione di chip. I due hanno un ottimo rapporto e Huang aveva ottenuto alcuni allentamenti, ma mai l’eliminazione completa del divieto. Per aggirarlo, le aziende cinesi hanno trovato due soluzioni: appoggiarsi legalmente a data center fuori dalla Cina, spesso nel Sudest asiatico, oppure importare illegalmente i microchip con vari trucchi.

Alice Huang era diventata dirigente di Megaspeed nel 2023 e, secondo quanto detto da Megaspeed domenica, avrebbe smesso di esserlo nell’agosto del 2025. L’azienda era stata la filiale di una società cinese di videogiochi online, e Huang ne aveva spostato gli investimenti sui data center. Ufficialmente non faceva nulla di illegale: Megaspeed importava i chip statunitensi e affittava la potenza di calcolo ad aziende cinesi senza trasferire i chip in Cina. Tra i suoi clienti c’era Alibaba, la principale azienda di e-commerce cinese.

Secondo quanto ipotizzato dalle indagini e da alcune inchieste giornalistiche però Megaspeed non si sarebbe limitata ad affittare la potenza di calcolo, ma sarebbe diventata uno snodo del contrabbando. Per dirigere questo traffico Alice Huang avrebbe sfruttato anche la sua vicinanza a Jensen Huang. Su di lei ci sono indagini in corso da tempo, mentre sul ruolo che Jensen Huang e Nvidia potrebbero aver avuto in tutto questo si sa ancora poco.

Un indizio a sostegno delle accuse a Megaspeed è la quantità di chip che l’azienda aveva comprato negli ultimi anni, per un valore di diversi miliardi di dollari. Una quantità giudicata eccessiva per gli scopi e l’estensione delle sue attività.

Stando a un’esclusiva del New York Times, già nel 2024 questa quantità fece nascere dei sospetti e il dipartimento del Commercio statunitense inviò dei funzionari in un data center di Megaspeed in Malaysia, per verificare che i microchip venduti fossero davvero lì. Furono trovati, ma erano ancora negli imballaggi, cosa che fece nascere il sospetto che i chip transitassero dal data center ma poi venissero inviati in Cina.

Venerdì Bloomberg ha scritto che, secondo documenti di cui è venuto in possesso, un’azienda cinese fondata da Alice Huang nel 2015 si sarebbe procurata chip di Nvidia arrivati in Cina di contrabbando, poi installati in un data center di Shanghai legato a Megaspeed. Bloomberg dice che ci sono prove per dire che i microchip siano stati importati per «una larga rete di aziende con al centro Alice Huang».

Venerdì il segretario al Tesoro Scott Bessent ha accusato pubblicamente il dipartimento del Commercio e il suo segretario, Howard Lutnick, di non aver agito tempestivamente per inserire Megaspeed nell’elenco delle aziende che non possono acquistare prodotti tecnologici dalle società statunitensi senza una precedente approvazione del governo.

Sempre secondo un’inchiesta del New York Times, Nvidia avrebbe avuto un ruolo nel mancato intervento del dipartimento del Commercio degli Stati Uniti, che pure stava indagando sulle attività di contrabbando di Megaspeed e Alice Huang.

Secondo il New York Times, ad agosto dell’anno scorso Tim Teter, il consulente legale generale di Nvidia, contattò direttamente alcuni agenti del dipartimento del Commercio coinvolti nell’indagine su Megaspeed, chiedendo di incontrarli per parlare del caso: la cosa insolita è che nella mail diceva di aver ricevuto il permesso di contattarli dal loro capo, Jeff Kessler, uno dei principali dirigenti del dipartimento, nominato da Trump.

Nonostante la pressione legata al nome di Kessler, gli agenti del dipartimento del Commercio negarono a Teter l’incontro, ma non ebbero tempo di pensare ulteriormente a come gestire la cosa perché l’indagine gli fu tolta, e fu spostata al dipartimento di Giustizia, dove è ancora in corso. Dell’indagine del dipartimento di Giustizia non si sa al momento niente.

Il New York Times ha scritto che «non è chiaro cosa abbia spinto Teter a rivolgersi al dipartimento, ma le recenti rivelazioni sulla relazione ammessa da Jensen Huang con una dirigente di Megaspeed non hanno fatto altro che aumentare l’attenzione sul ruolo di Nvidia nell’influenzare le politiche relative alla vendita di chip alla Cina».

Non è chiaro se Jensen Huang fosse al corrente della presunta attività di contrabbando di Megaspeed, e se sia intervenuto per facilitarla e ostacolare le indagini del dipartimento del Commercio, ma se dovesse venire fuori che è successo sarebbe uno scandalo enorme, non solo per Nvidia ma soprattutto per il governo statunitense.

articles.body:
A pochi giorni dal collasso globale di Microsoft e dal blocco a terra di tutti i voli, le infrastrutture digitali negli Stati Uniti si fermano di nuovo. Le principali banche americane - tra cui JpMorgan-Chase Bank of America, Wells Fargo e U.S. Bank - hanno riscontrato diffusi disservizi nei servizi di banking online e nelle procedure di accesso. Una sequenza di eventi che, sebbene al momento privi di collegamento, dimostra la fragilità di un intero sistema.

E nuovi disagi anche per il trasporto aereo americano. United Airlines segnala un'interruzione generalizzata dei suoi sistemi. "Ci scusiamo per l'inconveniente. Siamo a conoscenza dell'interruzione del sistema su vasta scala e i nostri team si stanno impegnando al massimo per ripristinare il corretto funzionamento nel minor tempo possibile", mette in evidenza United Airlines su X.

Non ci sono indicazioni che l'interruzione dei sistemi sia un cyberattacco. Lo ha detto un portavoce di United Airlines citando alcune fonti. "Stiamo risolvendo un problema tecnico che riguarda i voli in partenza. Non c'è alcun impatto sui voli in corso", ha messo in evidenza United Airlines.

Poco dopo United Airlines ha affermato di aver risolto il problema tecnico che ha causato ritardi ai suoi voli.

Anche Chase Bank afferma che i disservizi ai suoi sistemi sarebbero dovuti a un "problema temporaneo causato da un bug nel suo software" che potrebbe provocare disagi ad altre banche. La banca precisa che non si tratta di un "problema sistemico" né di un cyberattacco. "JPMorgan Chase ha riscontrato un problema temporaneo legato a un bug del software nei sistemi hardware locali. Non ci sono prove che si tratti di un attacco informatico. L'assistenza ad alcuni clienti sta richiedendo più tempo del solito", afferma Chase Bank. "Qualora le transazioni con altre banche fossero coinvolte, questi istituti potrebbero essere stati interessati ma non si tratta di un problema sistemico", ha messo in evidenza.

Sono stati gli utenti in mattinata a segnalare alle banche le difficoltà che stavano riscontrando: migliaia di persone che hanno lamentato difficoltà nell'accesso tramite web e app mobile, nonché problemi con i trasferimenti di denaro. La banca più colpita è stata JpMorgan Chase con oltre 4.600 4.600 segnalazioni, seguita da Bank of America con oltre 2.000.

L'assistenza di Chase è stata la più tempestiva ad intervenire prima con un messaggio agli utenti e poi con l'assistenza che ha confermato il disservizio, dichiarando di essere al lavoro per risolvere un problema tecnico che sta interessando le piattaforme di banking online.

"A causa di un problema tecnico, il completamento di alcune transazioni sta richiedendo più tempo del solito, ma i clienti continuano ad avere accesso ai propri conti e ai propri fondi», ha dichiarato l'istituto in un comunicato. "Stiamo lavorando per risolvere la situazione il più rapidamente possibile". Mentre una fonte informata ha spiegato a Fox Business che si tratta di "un bug tecnico, non un problema informatico".

Per ora insomma non ci sarebbe alcuna conferma che possa esserci un attacco informatico dietro i disservizi, e le verifiche condotte dalle stesse banche e dalle autorità finanziarie continuano ad indicare che il problema può essere stato causato da guasti tecnici interni, escludendo un'azione coordinata da parte di hacker.

Intanto la banca centrale americana, la Federal Reserve, ha assicurato che i suoi sistemi interbancari (Fedwire, FedACH e FedNow) funzionano regolarmente senza anomalie. Questo potrebbe confermare che il blocco riguarda i portali di accesso per i clienti (siti web e app) e non le reti fondamentali del sistema finanziario. Le banche hanno, inoltre, rassicurato i correntisti sul fatto che i fondi e i dati sensibili non sono stati compromessi, precisando che i team tecnici stanno lavorando per ripristinare la piena operatività.

Cnn, 'per le banche Usa un problema tecnico iniziato a Chase e che ha avuto ricadute

Il problema alle app e a servizi di alcune delle maggiori banche americane sarebbe tecnico e sarebbe stato iniziato da un'interruzione in casa Chase che avrebbe poi avuto ripercussioni sulle altre banche. Lo riporta Cnn citando alcune fonti.

articles.preview: Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed.
articles.body:
The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.

“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.
